cells.tense: Two things are asking for you at once, and you're holding both with your hands steady.
cells.ask: Name one amount you'd release today, say it to the person it belongs to, and keep hold of only what's yours to keep.
cells.core: Two things need you right now and you're not choosing between them — you're holding both, and from the outside it looks easy. It isn't. It's exact. You water what's dry, leave alone what's already fine, and do it without making a speech.\n\nWhat's arriving is another of those, and you'll meet it the way you've met the others. The part worth noticing: when something you've tended comes good, you let go of it cleanly. No clinging, no second-guessing. You finish, and finishing feels like relief, not like losing. That's the whole trick, and you already have it. Keep the loose grip.
cells.sheetLine: You finish things and let them go, and that's the trick.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady, responsible care
cells.place: Where what's arriving meets you at the threshold

cells.tense: You're already standing in a future where this has gone wrong, and you're tending to it before it has happened.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been watching ahead of time, and don't touch it for a day — no checking, no arranging, no fixing what hasn't broken.
cells.core:
You've got the future in your hands already. You can see the version where the thing dries up, or the person leaves, or you're left holding it alone — and you've started tending to that version now. Extra care, extra time, extra watching.

Here's the cost. None of that energy reaches the thing actually in front of you, because it's all going to a day that hasn't come. You're not overworked. You're working on the wrong day. What's in front of you is smaller and more real than what you're bracing for, and it can wait an afternoon while you stop prepping for it.

Let it be fine today. It usually is.
cells.sheetLine: You're caring for a day that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.verb: Tending what's growing with steady, responsible care

cells.tense: Something has been sitting at your door, and you've been leaving it there so long you stopped hearing the knock.
cells.ask: Take one small thing you put down — a plant, a page, a call — and touch it once this week, badly, for five minutes.
cells.core:
There's something at the edge of your life asking to be picked up, and you've been looking past it. The setting-down made sense once. Now it's just where you stand: new things arrive and you watch them arrive instead of reaching for them, and the watching gets called being realistic.

But the reach in you didn't go anywhere. It's running with nothing near it — that's the space between you and someone who was never in this. What's stalled is the starting, not the caring.

You don't need a big reason to pick something up again. You need one small, unimpressive act of care, done badly, this week. The charge comes back through the doing, not before it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped picking things up, and it looked like being sensible.

cells.tense: You're already the one holding this together, and you've been describing it as nobody in particular doing anything.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to one person, the one thing you've been keeping alive that no one has thanked you for keeping alive.
cells.core:
You're the one who remembers the appointments, checks the balances, waters it, calls back. That's tending, and it's running right now. But ask you about it and it becomes just how things are — as if the plants watered themselves and the invitations went out on their own.

People around you feel the shape of it. They'd tell you, if pressed, that things stay steady because you're there. You're the last to say it. When something you've carried finally lands, you hand the credit off as fast as it came to you.

It's the credit that's missing, not the care. Say one true sentence about what you've kept alive, once, and let it be heard instead of waved off. Finishing gets easier after that.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it alive, then call it nothing.
